title: Observation–Control Mismatch in Host–Microbiome Systems: When Can Microbiome Differences Be Safely Ignored?
content: The intestinal microbiome is a high-dimensional ecological system, but neither host physiology nor clinical measurement has access to all of that detail. Functional redundancy, ecological filtering and niche construction explain why taxonomically different communities can converge on similar functions or host phenotypes, yet they do not answer a separate decision problem: when can microbiome differences be safely ignored for intervention selection? Here I propose Host-Microbiome Projection-Selection Duality (HMPSD) as a microbiome-specific decision-theoretic framework for this problem. HMPSD distinguishes observational equivalence from control sufficiency. An observational class is benign when all states assigned to that class share at least one intervention whose expected loss lies within a predeclared acceptable margin of the best available option. Observation-control mismatch occurs when no such common acceptable action exists, so treating the class as homogeneous necessarily sacrifices meaningful outcome in at least part of the class. The framework does not claim a new general theory of decision making, nor does it require complete reconstruction of an endogenous host observation operator. Rather than primarily asking how to learn an optimal individualized treatment rule, HMPSD poses the complementary decision-sufficiency problem: which biological distinctions may a predefined microbiome representation safely discard without destroying a shared acceptable action? Experimental proxies, dynamic challenge responses and host-boundary measurements are valuable only to the extent that they preserve or improve prospective treatment choice. The intestinal boundary provides the biological basis for this formulation because microbial activity is compressed into epithelial, immune, neural and metabolic consequences, while host-controlled niche variables expand through ecological selection to reorganize many taxa. HMPSD generates task-bounded, falsifiable hypotheses rather than a universal existence claim. It can first be screened retrospectively in multi-intervention datasets and then tested prospectively in defined communities or gnotobiotic systems using predeclared observation operators, equivalence margins, intervention panels and replication. If observational classes repeatedly admit a shared acceptable action, the lost microbial detail is benign for that task. If matched states reproducibly require incompatible controls, static representation is control-insufficient and additional dynamic or boundary-state information is justified.
